name: Umar Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential, and I’d like both your public view and your private one.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Umar Young, twenty-seven. I lead a carpentry crew on building sites and live alone in a rented flat. I’ve kept a few months of expenses aside; my mother taught me not to spend next month’s wages before they arrive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through an ordinary workday. What do you enjoy and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I arrive before the crew, check the drawings and make sure the timber is stacked where we can work safely. I like teaching a new hand how to fit a frame properly instead of hiding a bad gap with trim. I don’t enjoy rushing to finish paperwork at the end, and the noise can leave me with a headache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say I’m not against a tool that catches a wrong count on a materials sheet. I’d still put a tape on the wall and check the timber before the crew cuts anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t think a small change will touch the main work I do. My savings would cover a short gap between sites, and there are a couple of builders nearby where I could ask for hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and compare any computer count with the signed paper order. I’d continue saving after payday instead of buying a new car just because the account looks healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a tool that can be checked. I still keep a reserve because even a good trade has quiet weeks between contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a materials count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the first few orders against the delivery and write down anything missing. If the list keeps matching, I’d be willing to use it for the routine count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work would you still insist on checking in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d measure the opening and check the wall for movement myself. A plan can’t show me what happened after the surveyor left the site.

say: I’m open to a tool that catches a **wrong materials count**.
I still measure the wall before the crew **cuts timber**.
think: I don’t expect a small change to affect my **main site work**.
I can cover a short gap with **my savings** and nearby employers.
do: Keep leading the **crew** and compare computer counts with signed orders.
Record any missing timber on the **delivery slip**.
feel: I feel **calm** about a tool I can check.
S0.quote: A plan can’t show me what happened after the surveyor left the site.
fieldNote: Umar values **direct inspection** and will test a count before trusting it.
He has a modest reserve and nearby contacts, so routine change feels **manageable**.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on active jobs
Compare the computer count with early materials deliveries
Continue saving part of each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office can use a schedule tool, but the crew needs to know whether the delivery date is real. I don’t want five people standing around because a screen forgot that another trade is still in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I handle some planning and records as crew lead, so I expect those tasks to change. I’m not eager to learn a new system, but I could do it if the foreman shows me how it helps on the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman to demonstrate the schedule tool using a job we already understand. I’d keep the crew’s carpentry work steady and check the roster before making a large purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because my paperwork could change, but I have time to learn if someone teaches me. I wouldn’t call every new screen progress until it proves useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see during that demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to see it handle a change in delivery and leave time for our measurements. If the foreman can show the old and new schedule side by side, I’ll understand what the tool actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this card say that office changes cause fewer construction sites to open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t claim that. I’d look at the contractor’s booked work and local openings rather than blame AI for something the card doesn’t say.

say: I’d want the schedule to show a **real delivery date**.
I don’t want the crew waiting because another trade is **still working**.
think: I handle some planning and records, and I expect **those tasks to change**.
I can learn a system if the foreman shows how it helps **on site**.
do: Ask the **foreman** to demonstrate the schedule tool on a familiar job.
Check my roster before making a large **purchase**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but I can learn with a practical demonstration.
S1.quote: I wouldn’t call every new screen progress until it proves useful.
fieldNote: Umar needs a **hands-on demonstration** before adopting a new system.
He avoids attributing fewer starts to AI without **evidence from the contractor**, and waits for the real roster.

steps.text: Learn the schedule tool from the foreman on a familiar job
Keep leading carpentry work on active sites
Wait for the roster before making a large purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew to listen for what the contractor actually says about the next jobs. We should keep the paper records straight and not pass around a rumor as if someone had already been dismissed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take the planning and records in my lead role by 2028. Robots reach the hands-on work in 2031, so I can’t tell myself carpentry will stay safe just because I’m good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and add to the savings I already have. In 2029 I’d ask for the contractor’s confirmed schedule and contact nearby builders if my hours had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short enough to make me anxious about pay, though my savings buy some time. I know what I can cut, but I can’t guarantee a builder has an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could applying to another builder protect you from the 2031 robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d treat it as a way to get paid while there is work, not protection from the same change. If a local builder has a real job in 2029, I’d call and ask what hours they offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop putting money toward a newer car and keep rent, food and transport covered. I’m single, so I can make a spending change without first moving children or a partner.

say: I’d ask what the contractor says about **confirmed jobs**.
I’d keep records straight and avoid repeating **dismissal rumors**.
think: I expect AGI to take records and planning in **my lead role** by 2028.
I can’t say carpentry stays safe when **robots arrive in 2031**.
do: Keep working and add to my current **savings**.
Contact **local builders** if my hours have fallen.
feel: I feel **anxious about pay**, though my savings buy some time.
S2.quote: I can’t tell myself carpentry will stay safe just because I’m good at it.
fieldNote: Umar sees the robot date as relevant even with strong **craft skill**.
He would use savings and reduce purchases rather than claim a **guaranteed vacancy**.

steps.text: Keep leading the current crew while there is work
Add to my current savings before hours fall
Contact nearby builders if my hours fall in 2029
Stop saving toward a newer car if pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough time for managers to tell crews what is changing and explain new steps. I’d rather hear a plain answer at the toolbox meeting than a notice after a shift has disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI can take the planning and record side by 2031, then robots reach the carpentry around 2034. I have more time than in the fast picture, but there’s no promise that other local work will be waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have the foreman show me the system before it becomes part of every job. In 2032 I’d check my hours and savings, and then contact builders nearby if my current crew was smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me some breathing room, and I’m still anxious about both parts of the job. I’d use the extra time carefully instead of treating it as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years of warning differ from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get more paydays to save and more time to watch what the contractor actually changes. I’d rather learn from someone on my site than borrow money for a course before I know what is useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would construction office planning protect you after AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call planning safe if AGI can do the thinking work. I’d learn enough to handle the current tools and keep asking which jobs a real builder needs filled.

say: I’d want managers to explain changes at the **toolbox meeting**.
I’d rather hear a plain answer before a shift **disappears**.
think: I expect AGI to take planning and records by **2031**.
I have more time, but I can’t assume **another job will wait**.
do: Ask the **foreman** to show me the system before it is used widely.
Check my hours and savings in **2032**.
Contact **nearby builders** if my crew becomes smaller.
feel: I feel **anxious but less rushed** than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I’d rather learn from someone on my site than borrow money for a course before I know what is useful.
fieldNote: Umar prefers **learning on site** to debt-funded training, and asks a foreman for direct guidance.
He recognizes that planning is exposed and will check for **real openings**.

steps.text: Learn the new system from the foreman on active jobs
Continue saving during the additional warning years
Contact nearby builders if the crew shrinks after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is a long runway, but crews should still prepare instead of assuming nothing will happen. I’d keep doing careful work and learn a tool after it has been tested on a real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save more in ten years, but the thinking part of my lead job still changes in 2036. Robots reach carpentry around 2039, and I don’t know what kind of work nearby builders will still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading my crew, add to the reserve, and learn tools when the foreman has checked them. In 2037 I’d review the jobs in the area and call nearby builders if the contractor had reduced my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to save and observe, which feels better than two. I’m still uneasy about the robot date because it reaches the craft work I rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to decide before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d decide how much of my pay to save and whether I want to move to a place with more building work. I’m single, so I can make that choice for myself, but I’d want to visit first rather than move on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a long course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take short training if it is tied to a job I can see. I wouldn’t spend my reserve on a course promising office work after AGI, since planning is part of what changes.

say: I’d use the **long runway** to prepare rather than assume nothing will happen.
I’d learn a tool after someone tests it on a **real site**.
think: I could build more savings before **2036**.
I don’t know what nearby builders will need after **robots arrive**.
do: Keep leading my crew while **contracts continue**.
Add to my **reserve** and learn tested tools.
Review local jobs in 2037 and call builders if my **hours fall**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the robot date, despite having time to prepare.
S4.quote: I’d say ten years is a long runway, but crews should still prepare instead of assuming nothing will happen.
fieldNote: Umar treats a decade as **useful warning**, not proof of safety, and plans to check in regularly.
He would consider moving only after checking **actual local work**.

steps.text: Keep leading the current crew while contracts continue
Add to my reserve from current wages
Learn tools after a foreman tests them on site
Visit a busier area before deciding whether to move

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is not much time to prepare for the office change and the 2031 robot date. Clear notice about the contractor’s work and a chance to learn tools during paid hours would help me decide what to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask what jobs are actually available nearby when a contract ends. People can talk about adapting, but I need to know whether there is a builder with real hours before I move or retrain.

headlineQuote: I’d ask what jobs are actually available nearby when a contract ends.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old crew lead** with strong carpentry skills and a trade certificate.
He lives alone, earns typical pay, and has **a few months saved**.
He avoids unfamiliar technology but will learn a **proven tool** from a foreman on site.
Some local builders and a savings reserve give him options, though robots eventually threaten **his craft work**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Umar most because the short warning leaves little time before the robot date.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice about **contractor work** and paid training time would help Umar plan his next step.
